metadata.title: Gradient Descent Step
metadata.subject: Mathematics
metadata.objective: Let a learner who knows algebra but not calculus see why a step goes opposite the gradient.
misconceptions: A larger learning rate is always better
expectedUnderstanding: The step direction opposes the local gradient
The step length is scaled by the learning rate
A larger step can overshoot and increase the cost

primitives.text: Gradient descent: step opposite the slope

checkpoints.title: Small step
checkpoints.body: Set the rate to 0.15. The arrow is short and the next point is still to the right of the minimum.

checkpoints.title: Landing on the minimum
checkpoints.body: Set the rate to 0.5. The step is 1.6 - 0.5 x 3.2 = 0, so the next point lands at the minimum.

checkpoints.title: Overshoot
checkpoints.body: Set the rate to 1.2. The step overshoots to negative x, and the next point is higher than the starting point: a bigger step is not always better.

narration.text: The tangent has positive slope, so the gradient points uphill to the right. The step arrow points left.
At rate 0.5 the step lands exactly at the minimum.
At a large rate the step overshoots; the new point climbs the other side of the parabola.

fallback.text: At the marked point the slope is positive, so the gradient points uphill to the right. A gradient-descent step moves left, scaled by the learning rate. Rate 0.5 lands at the minimum; a larger rate overshoots and can raise the cost.

accessibility.alt: A parabola with a marked point on its right branch, a positive tangent, and a leftward step arrow whose length grows with the learning-rate slider; a vertical line projects the updated point onto the curve.
